memory_candidates.content: When one dispatched agent (a writer) can rewrite a file mid-read by a concurrently-dispatched sibling (a reader) within the same orchestration cycle, the correct fix is TWO complementary layers, not one: (1) a routine, unconditional 'landed-change' sentinel from the writer side (a small JSON file keyed by the writer's own completion time, with a freshness rule relative to the reader's OWN dispatch_start_ts, never dispatch-build time) that explains WHY something changed and provides fast awareness; and (2) a narrow pre-write re-read obligation on the reader side, scoped to only the specific section it is about to act on, immediately before its first write, that actually CATCHES a tear landing between two reads before any sentinel exists. The sentinel alone cannot prevent a stale write (write-after-the-fact); the re-read alone gives no attribution for why the text changed. Treat them as answering different questions, not as redundant.

When a decision cannot be expressed at the point a dispatch file is BUILT because the orchestrator hasn't yet decided which other tasks get dispatched this cycle (e.g. aux-row emission runs before admission/bucketing), the cheapest correct resolution is often to emit the conditional instruction UNCONDITIONALLY rather than deferring the write or reordering the decision pipeline -- provided the instruction is cheap and inert when its precondition doesn't hold (e.g. 'write a sentinel file, even if no one will read it'). This avoids threading new flags through multiple script layers and avoids splitting an existing decision block's documented structure. Reach for conditional/deferred emission only when the unconditional write has a real cost or side effect.
